summary.text: Using binary recurrences for the prime-power generating series \(B\), the proof constructs a logarithmic-derivative series \(D\) with nonnegative coefficients and defines \(C\) by \(2C'=DC\), so all coefficients of \(C\) are nonnegative; since \(B'=DB\) and the constant terms agree, a formal-power-series uniqueness argument gives \(C^2=B\). Multiplicativity then identifies the desired square root at \(n\) with \(\prod_p C_{v_p(n)}\), which is nonnegative.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S(e)=\sum_{r\ge 0}\left\lfloor\frac e{2^r}\right\rfloor
\qquad(e\ge 0).
\]
The sum is finite, since its terms vanish once \(2^r>e\). Define
\[
b_e=2^{S(e)}.
\]
Thus the multiplicative function A046644, which we denote by \(B_{\rm ar}\), is
\[
B_{\rm ar}(n)=\prod_{p}b_{v_p(n)}
 =\prod_p 2^{S(v_p(n))}
\quad(n\ge1),
\]
and \(B_{\rm ar}(0)=0\). The product is over the finitely many primes dividing \(n\). We will construct a nonnegative multiplicative function \(G\) such that
\[
G*G=B_{\rm ar},
\]
where \(*\) denotes Dirichlet convolution. We will then show that \(G\) is exactly the recursively defined Dirichlet-convolution square root whose numerators form A317940.

First we study the local sequence \((b_e)_{e\ge0}\). Splitting off the term with \(r=0\) in the definition of \(S\) gives
\[
S(2m)=2m+S(m),\qquad S(2m+1)=2m+1+S(m).
\]
Indeed, for \(r\ge1\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{2m}{2^r}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac m{2^{r-1}}\right\rfloor,
\qquad
\left\lfloor\frac{2m+1}{2^r}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac m{2^{r-1}}\right\rfloor.
\]
Consequently,
\[
b_{2m}=4^m b_m,
\qquad
b_{2m+1}=2\,4^m b_m. \tag{1}
\]
Also \(b_0=1\).

We next construct the coefficients of the logarithmic derivative of the ordinary generating series of the \(b_e\)'s. Define rational numbers \(M_r\) recursively by
\[
M_0=0,
\]
and, for \(r>0\),
\[
M_r=
\begin{cases}
2^r,&r\text{ odd},\\
2^{r+1}M_{r/2}-2^r,&r\text{ even}.
\end{cases} \tag{2}
\]
This is a valid recursion because in the positive even case \(r/2<r\). Put
\[
d_k=M_{k+1}\qquad(k\ge0). \tag{3}
\]

All the \(d_k\) are nonnegative. In fact, the stronger assertion
\[
M_r\ge1\qquad(r>0) \tag{4}
\]
holds by strong induction on \(r\). If \(r\) is odd, then \(M_r=2^r\ge1\). If \(r\) is positive and even, then \(r\ge2\), and the induction hypothesis gives \(M_{r/2}\ge1\). Hence
\[
M_r=2^{r+1}M_{r/2}-2^r
    =2^r(2M_{r/2}-1)
    \ge 2^r\ge1.
\]
Thus \(d_k=M_{k+1}\ge1\), in particular \(d_k\ge0\), for every \(k\ge0\).

Two parity formulas for the \(d_k\)'s follow immediately from (2). For \(j\ge0\), since \(2j+1\) is odd,
\[
d_{2j}=M_{2j+1}=2^{2j+1}=2\,4^j. \tag{5}
\]
Since \(2j+2=2(j+1)\) is positive and even,
\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{2j+1}
 &=M_{2j+2}\\
 &=2^{2j+3}M_{j+1}-2^{2j+2}\\
 &=8\,4^j d_j-4\,4^j. 
\end{aligned} \tag{6}
\]

The key identity is
\[
N b_N=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}d_k b_{N-1-k}
\qquad(N\ge0), \tag{7}
\]
where for \(N=0\) the sum is empty. We prove this by strong induction on \(N\), separating odd and even \(N\). The assertion is immediate for \(N=0\).

Suppose first that \(N=2n+1\). In the sum on the right of (7), split \(k\) into the even indices \(k=2j\), where \(0\le j\le n\), and the odd indices \(k=2j+1\), where \(0\le j<n\). By (1) and (5), the sum over the even indices is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j=0}^{n}d_{2j}b_{2n-2j}
 &=\sum_{j=0}^{n}(2\,4^j)(4^{n-j}b_{n-j})\\
 &=2\,4^n\sum_{j=0}^{n}b_{n-j}. \tag{8}
\end{aligned}
\]
For an odd index, (1) and (6) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{2j+1}b_{2n-(2j+1)}
 &=(8\,4^j d_j-4\,4^j)
   b_{2(n-1-j)+1}\\
 &=(8\,4^j d_j-4\,4^j)
   (2\,4^{n-1-j}b_{n-1-j})\\
 &=4^{n+1}d_jb_{n-1-j}-2\,4^n b_{n-1-j}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore the sum over all odd indices is
\[
4^{n+1}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}d_jb_{n-1-j}
-2\,4^n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}b_{n-1-j}. \tag{9}
\]
By the induction hypothesis applied to \(n<2n+1\),
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}d_jb_{n-1-j}=n b_n.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{n}b_{n-j}-\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}b_{n-1-j}=b_n.
\]
Adding (8) and (9), we thus obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=0}^{2n}d_kb_{2n-k}
 &=2\,4^n b_n+4^{n+1}n b_n\\
 &=(2n+1)(2\,4^n b_n)\\
 &=(2n+1)b_{2n+1},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last equality uses (1). This proves (7) for odd \(N\).

Now suppose that \(N=2m\), where \(m\ge1\). There are \(m\) even indices \(k=2j\) and \(m\) odd indices \(k=2j+1\), with \(0\le j<m\). For the even indices, (1) and (5) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{2j}b_{2m-1-2j}
 &=(2\,4^j)b_{2(m-1-j)+1}\\
 &=(2\,4^j)(2\,4^{m-1-j}b_{m-1-j})\\
 &=4^m b_{m-1-j}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus their total contribution is
\[
4^m\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}b_{m-1-j}. \tag{10}
\]
For the odd indices, (1) and (6) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{2j+1}b_{2m-1-(2j+1)}
 &=(8\,4^j d_j-4\,4^j)b_{2(m-1-j)}\\
 &=(8\,4^j d_j-4\,4^j)
   (4^{m-1-j}b_{m-1-j})\\
 &=2\,4^m d_jb_{m-1-j}-4^m b_{m-1-j}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Their total contribution is therefore
\[
2\,4^m\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}d_jb_{m-1-j}
-4^m\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}b_{m-1-j}. \tag{11}
\]
The last term in (11) cancels (10). The induction hypothesis applied to \(m<2m\) says that the remaining convolution sum equals \(m b_m\). Hence
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{2m-1}d_kb_{2m-1-k}
 =2\,4^m m b_m
 =(2m)b_{2m},
\]
using \(b_{2m}=4^m b_m\). This completes the proof of (7).

Introduce the formal power series
\[
B(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}b_nx^n,
\qquad
D(x)=\sum_{k\ge0}d_kx^k.
\]
The coefficient of \(x^{N-1}\) in \(D(x)B(x)\) is the right side of (7), while its coefficient in \(B'(x)\) is \(Nb_N\). Thus (7) is precisely the formal differential equation
\[
B'(x)=D(x)B(x). \tag{12}
\]

We now construct a square root of \(B(x)\) whose coefficients are nonnegative. Define \(c_0=1\), and for \(n\ge1\) define recursively
\[
c_n=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}d_kc_{n-1-k}. \tag{13}
\]
Every \(d_k\) is nonnegative, and \(2n>0\). Therefore a straightforward induction on \(n\) shows
\[
c_n\ge0\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{14}
\]
Indeed, \(c_0=1\), and if all earlier \(c_i\)'s are nonnegative, every summand in (13) is nonnegative.

Let
\[
C(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_nx^n.
\]
For every \(n\ge0\), equation (13), with \(n+1\) in place of \(n\), says
\[
2(n+1)c_{n+1}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}d_kc_{n-k}.
\]
Comparing coefficients gives
\[
2C'(x)=D(x)C(x). \tag{15}
\]
We claim that
\[
C(x)^2=B(x). \tag{16}
\]
Set \(H(x)=C(x)^2-B(x)\). By the formal product rule and (12), (15),
\[
\begin{aligned}
H'(x)
 &=2C(x)C'(x)-B'(x)\\
 &=D(x)C(x)^2-D(x)B(x)\\
 &=D(x)H(x). \tag{17}
\end{aligned}
\]
Also the constant coefficient of \(H\) is
\[
c_0^2-b_0=1-1=0.
\]
A formal power series satisfying \(H'=DH\) and having zero constant coefficient must be zero. To see this directly, suppose inductively that the coefficients \(h_0,\dots,h_n\) of \(H\) vanish. The coefficient of \(x^n\) in \(DH\) is a sum of terms \(d_i h_{n-i}\), all of which vanish, whereas the coefficient of \(x^n\) in \(H'\) is \((n+1)h_{n+1}\). Since we work over \(\mathbb Q\), \(n+1\ne0\), so \(h_{n+1}=0\). Beginning with \(h_0=0\), induction gives \(H=0\), proving (16).

Comparing coefficients in (16), we obtain the local convolution identities
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{e}c_i c_{e-i}=b_e
\qquad(e\ge0). \tag{18}
\]

We now pass from prime-power exponents back to positive integers. Define
\[
G(n)=\prod_p c_{v_p(n)}\qquad(n\ge1),
\]
and put \(G(0)=0\). Since \(c_0=1\), only primes dividing \(n\) affect the product. Equation (14) immediately gives
\[
G(n)\ge0\qquad(n\ge1). \tag{19}
\]
The function \(G\) is multiplicative: if \(m\) and \(n\) are coprime, then for each prime \(p\), at most one of \(v_p(m),v_p(n)\) is positive, so
\[
c_{v_p(mn)}=c_{v_p(m)+v_p(n)}
 =c_{v_p(m)}c_{v_p(n)},
\]
because one of the two subscripts is zero and \(c_0=1\). Multiplying over \(p\) yields \(G(mn)=G(m)G(n)\). In particular,
\[
G(p^e)=c_e. \tag{20}
\]

The Dirichlet convolution of two multiplicative functions is multiplicative. On a prime power, its divisors are \(1,p,\dots,p^e\), and hence (18) and (20) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
(G*G)(p^e)
 &=\sum_{i=0}^{e}G(p^i)G(p^{e-i})\\
 &=\sum_{i=0}^{e}c_i c_{e-i}\\
 &=b_e\\
 &=B_{\rm ar}(p^e).
\end{aligned} \tag{21}
\]
Both \(G*G\) and \(B_{\rm ar}\) are multiplicative and agree on every prime power, so unique prime factorization implies that they agree on every positive integer:
\[
G*G=B_{\rm ar}. \tag{22}
\]

It remains to identify \(G\) with the rational sequence underlying A317940. Let \(f(0)=0\), \(f(1)=1\), and, for \(n>1\), let
\[
f(n)=\frac12\left(B_{\rm ar}(n)-
 \sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\1<d<n}}f(d)f(n/d)\right). \tag{23}
\]
This is the defining recurrence for the Dirichlet-convolution square root used in A317940.

From (22), for \(n>1\),
\[
B_{\rm ar}(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}G(d)G(n/d).
\]
Separate the divisors \(d=1\) and \(d=n\). Since \(G(1)=c_0=1\), these two endpoint terms are each \(G(n)\). Every other divisor satisfies \(1<d<n\). Thus
\[
B_{\rm ar}(n)=2G(n)+
 \sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\1<d<n}}G(d)G(n/d),
\]
or equivalently
\[
G(n)=\frac12\left(B_{\rm ar}(n)-
 \sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\1<d<n}}G(d)G(n/d)\right). \tag{24}
\]
Equations (23) and (24), together with \(f(0)=G(0)=0\) and \(f(1)=G(1)=1\), imply \(f(n)=G(n)\) for all \(n\) by strong induction. Indeed, when \(n>1\), every argument \(d\) and \(n/d\) occurring in the proper-divisor sum lies strictly between \(1\) and \(n\), so all those values of \(f\) and \(G\) agree by the induction hypothesis; the two recurrences then give the same value at \(n\).

Finally, for every \(n\ge1\), (19) gives
\[
f(n)=G(n)=\prod_p c_{v_p(n)}\ge0.
\]
Therefore every rational term whose numerator defines A317940 is nonnegative. In particular, its reduced numerator is nonnegative, proving that for every integer \(n\ge1\), \(a(n)\ge0\).
